guide.title: Killingly, Connecticut: Cotton Mills, a Diner, and a Tiffany Birthplace
guide.intro: Killingly was settled in 1700 and incorporated in 1708, beginning as a cluster of mill villages on the Five Mile and Quinebaug Rivers; English colonists first called the area "Aspinock" before Governor Gurdon Saltonstall suggested "Kellingly," later altered to Killingly. In the first half of the 19th century Killingly was the largest producer of cotton goods in Connecticut, and it later became known as "the curtain capital of the world." Mary Dixon Kies, born in South Killingly in 1752, received a U.S. patent in 1809 for weaving straw with silk and thread — often cited as the first patent issued to a woman in her own name. Charles Lewis Tiffany, founder of Tiffany & Company, was born in Killingly in 1812 and worked in his father's store and cotton mill before leaving for New York. Danielson has had a notable Laotian community since 1979, when the first refugee family arrived sponsored by a local couple.

sections.heading: Cotton, curtains, and a Tiffany birthplace
sections.body: Killingly was settled in 1700 and incorporated in 1708, beginning as a cluster of mill villages on the Five Mile and Quinebaug Rivers. In the first half of the 19th century Killingly was the largest producer of cotton goods in Connecticut, later known as "the curtain capital of the world." Mary Dixon Kies, born in South Killingly in 1752, received a U.S. patent in 1809 for weaving straw with silk and thread — often cited as the first patent issued to a woman in her own name; she is buried in Old South Killingly Cemetery. Charles Lewis Tiffany, founder of Tiffany & Company, was born in Killingly in 1812 and worked in his father's general store and cotton mill office before leaving for New York. The borough of Danielson, originally "Danielsonville" for Gen. James Danielson, has had a notable Laotian community since September 1979, when the first refugee family arrived sponsored by Daniel and Carolyn O'Leary — a heritage visible today in the borough's Lao restaurants.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Interstate 395 is the primary north-south corridor through Killingly, meeting US Route 6 and Route 101 near downtown Danielson; Route 12 also passes through and divides downtown. There is no passenger rail station in Killingly or Danielson; the Norwich and Worcester Railroad reached the village by 1840 and shaped Main Street's growth, but no passenger service remains. The nearest Connecticut rail service is CTrail Shore Line East at New London, reached by driving south on I-395. Metro-North's New Haven Line and the CTrail Hartford Line do not serve northeastern Connecticut at all.

faq.question: How do I get to Killingly?
faq.answer: By car — Interstate 395 is the main corridor, meeting US Route 6 and Route 101 near downtown Danielson. There is no passenger rail station in Killingly; the nearest Connecticut rail service is Shore Line East at New London.

faq.question: Is there a train to Killingly?
faq.answer: No. Killingly has no passenger rail station today, and Metro-North's New Haven Line and the CTrail Hartford Line do not serve northeastern Connecticut at all. Drive south on I-395 to reach Shore Line East at New London.

faq.question: What is the Danielson Main Street Historic District?
faq.answer: A 20-acre National Register district with more than 40 commercial buildings from about 1850-1920, including the 1901 Bugbee Memorial Library, the 1855 Westfield Congregational Church and the 1856 Attawaugan Hotel.

faq.question: Can I go skydiving in Killingly?
faq.answer: Yes — Skydive Danielson offers tandem jumps for first-timers at Danielson Airport, operating seasonally May through October, seven days a week.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Killingly?
faq.answer: No hotel or inn inside Killingly could be independently confirmed as bookable; travelers should check availability directly before planning around any single property.

places.name: Killingly Historical & Genealogical Center
places.summary: Housed in the Bugbee Memorial building, a local-history museum with changing exhibits, a biographical research library and a genealogical research center. Open Wednesdays and Saturdays 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

places.name: Old Furnace State Park
places.summary: A 367-acre state park named for a pre-Revolutionary iron furnace that sold horseshoes to the Continental Army. A roughly 3-mile blue-blazed trail crosses Furnace Brook and climbs Half Hill for views into Rhode Island; a shorter three-quarter-mile spur reaches an overlook. Free, year-round hiking, boating, fishing and hunting.

places.name: Killingly Pond State Park
places.summary: A 162-acre park on the western shore of Killingly Pond, which straddles the Connecticut-Rhode Island line. Open for boating, fishing, hiking and hunting.

places.name: Skydive Danielson
places.address: Danielson Airport, 41 Airport Road, Danielson, CT 06239
places.summary: A tandem skydiving operation open to first-timers, a member of the United States Parachute Association. Operates seasonally May through October, seven days a week; closed early November through mid-April. Plan on three to five hours at the dropzone.

places.name: Danielson Main Street Historic District
places.address: Main Street between the Five Mile River and Spring Street, Danielson, CT 06239
places.summary: A 20-acre National Register district with more than 40 mostly commercial buildings from about 1850-1920, including the 1901 Bugbee Memorial Library, the 1855 Westfield Congregational Church, the 1902 Danielson Methodist Church and the 1856 Attawaugan Hotel. A publicly walkable streetscape; downtown construction may affect parking during the ongoing Brickyard Plaza project.
